youtube.baslik: The Ossicular Chain: Malleus, Incus and Stapes | Lesson 20 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
We describe the parts of the three middle ear ossicles, the malleus, incus and stapes, the joints between them, and how the stapes footplate sits in the oval window. With examples, we see how the chain moves and how chain problems show up on the tympanogram.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Gelfand, Essentials of Audiology; Zemlin, Speech and Hearing Science: Anatomy and Physiology; Seikel, King and Drumright, Anatomy and Physiology for Speech, Language, and Hearing; Jerger, Clinical experience with impedance audiometry (1970).

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.baslik: The *Ossicular Chain*: Malleus, Incus and Stapes
sahneler.alt: Parts, joints and the oval window
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson, we meet the three tiny bones of the middle ear, the ossicles.
We will look at the parts of the malleus, incus and stapes, the joints between them and how the chain connects to the oval window.
In the middle ear, three tiny bones span the space between the tympanic membrane and the inner ear: the ossicles.
The first bone, attached to the inner surface of the membrane, is the malleus, or hammer.
The middle bone is the incus, or anvil.
The last link is the stapes, or stirrup, named for its shape, which resembles a riding stirrup.
The footplate of the stapes sits in the fenestra vestibuli, or oval window, the entrance to the inner ear.
Together, the three bones form a bridge that carries the vibration of the membrane into the inner ear fluids.
The malleus is the longest bone in the chain.
The stapes, at about three millimeters high, is the smallest bone in the human body.
These bones are so small that all three together could fit on a fingertip.
At birth, the ossicles have almost reached their adult size.
The chain hangs from the middle ear walls by fine ligaments and two small muscles, so it can vibrate freely.

maddeler.metin: Malleus and incus: mostly the _1st pharyngeal arch_

cumleler: Most of the malleus and incus develops from the cartilage of the first pharyngeal arch in the embryo.
The stapes comes mainly from the second pharyngeal arch.
The inner surface of the stapes footplate, facing the inner ear, develops partly from the otic capsule.
That is why, in some developmental syndromes affecting the pharyngeal arches, outer ear and ossicle anomalies can occur together.
The rounded head of the malleus, the caput, sits in the attic, the upper part of the middle ear.
The head is joined to the handle by a thin neck, the collum.
The manubrium, or handle, is embedded in the fibrous layer of the tympanic membrane, and its tip forms the umbo.
The processus lateralis, or lateral process, at the top of the handle is the small bump seen on otoscopy.
The processus anterior, or anterior process, is attached by a ligament to the anterior wall of the middle ear.
The tendon of the tensor tympani muscle attaches to the upper part of the manubrium.
The body of the incus, the corpus, forms a joint with the head of the malleus.
These two parts sit together in the attic and are usually not visible on otoscopy.
The short process, the crus breve, points backward and is held by a ligament in a small pit on the posterior wall of the attic.
The long process, the crus longum, runs downward, parallel to the manubrium.
At the tip of the long process is a small, lentil-shaped projection: the processus lenticularis.
This projection forms a joint with the head of the stapes.
Being thin with a poor blood supply, the long process of the incus is among the parts most prone to erosion in chronic middle ear disease.
The stapes is the last and smallest bone of the chain.
Its head, the caput, forms a joint with the lenticular process of the incus, followed by a short neck.
Two limbs branch off from the neck, one anterior and one posterior: the crus anterius and the crus posterius.
The limbs join an oval footplate of about three square millimeters, called the basis stapedis.
The footplate sits in the fenestra vestibuli and is held at its edges by the ligamentum anulare, the annular ligament.
The tendon of the stapedius muscle attaches to the neck of the stapes from behind.
The flexible annular ligament lets the footplate move in and out within the window.
Now let us summarize the three bones in one table.
The malleus has a head, a neck and a handle; it connects to the eardrum by its handle and to the incus by its head.
The incus has a body, a short process and a long process; it forms a bridge between the malleus and the stapes.
The stapes has a head, two crura and a footplate; it passes the vibration it receives from the incus to the oval window.

notlar.metin: Incus to stapes: synovial, ball and socket

cumleler: The ossicles are connected to each other by two true joints.
The joint between the head of the malleus and the body of the incus is the incudomalleolar joint, a saddle-shaped synovial joint.
This joint is quite tight, so the malleus and incus often move as a single unit.
The joint between the lenticular process and the stapes head is the incudostapedial joint, a small ball-and-socket joint.
This joint is one of the most delicate points in the chain and can separate with trauma or disease.
The connection between the stapes footplate and the oval window is not a true joint but a fibrous ligament.
The fine ligaments that hold the chain in place also define its axis of rotation.
The ligaments holding the malleus from above and in front connect it to the roof of the attic and the anterior wall of the middle ear.
The posterior incudal ligament fixes the short process of the incus to the posterior wall of the attic.
The stapes footplate is attached to the rim of the oval window by the annular ligament we saw earlier.
The balanced tension of these ligaments keeps the chain both stable and mobile.
When the membrane moves inward, the malleus and incus rotate together, like a hinge.
This axis of rotation is the line from the anterior process of the malleus to the short process of the incus.
Because the manubrium is a little longer than the long process of the incus, the chain works like a small lever.
This lever ratio is about one point three to one, and it increases the force reaching the stapes.
At moderate sound levels, the stapes footplate moves in and out of the oval window like a piston.
When the footplate moves inward, the inner ear fluid is pushed and the round window bulges outward.
The main job of the chain is to transfer sound energy in the air efficiently into the fluid-filled inner ear.
Force collected over the large area of the membrane and delivered to the small stapes footplate raises the pressure about seventeen times.
The lever effect raises it by about another one point three times.
Together, these mechanisms provide a gain of about twenty five to thirty decibels.
In addition, two muscles attached to the chain can stiffen it for very loud sounds and reduce the energy passed to the inner ear.
We will look at these muscles and the acoustic reflex in detail in the next lesson.
The state of the chain is also reflected in the shape of the tympanogram; a normal chain gives a type A curve.

cumleler.yazi: If the chain stiffens, the curve becomes shallow and its peak drops; this is called type As.
cumleler.ses: If the chain stiffens, the curve becomes shallow and its peak drops; this is called type A S.

cumleler: Otosclerosis is an example; in this disease, abnormal bone forms around the stapes footplate and fixes it.
In otosclerosis, a Carhart notch around two thousand hertz may also be seen in bone conduction.

cumleler.yazi: If the chain is disrupted, say at the incudostapedial joint, the system becomes too flaccid and the peak is very high; this is type Ad.
cumleler.ses: If the chain is disrupted, say at the incudostapedial joint, the system becomes too flaccid and the peak is very high; this is type A D.

cumleler: With ossicular discontinuity, sound reaches the inner ear very weakly, and a large conductive hearing loss can result.
In these examples, bone conduction is usually preserved, and the audiogram shows a clear air-bone gap.

sahneler.metin: A type Ad curve is not always ossicular discontinuity; a thin or scarred eardrum also gives a high curve. Check otoscopy and the air-bone gap first.
cumleler: There is a common mistake when interpreting tympanograms.

cumleler.yazi: A type Ad curve with a very high peak does not always mean ossicular discontinuity.
cumleler.ses: A type A D curve with a very high peak does not always mean ossicular discontinuity.

cumleler: A membrane thinned or scarred after an old, healed perforation can give a similar curve.
To tell them apart, first look at otoscopy and check the air-bone gap on the audiogram.

cumleler.yazi: With an Ad curve caused by the membrane, there is usually no significant conductive loss; with discontinuity, a large gap is expected.
cumleler.ses: With an A D curve caused by the membrane, there is usually no significant conductive loss; with discontinuity, a large gap is expected.

cumleler: The malleus, incus and stapes form the ossicular chain, which carries the vibration of the membrane to the inner ear.
The stapes footplate sits in the fenestra vestibuli, or oval window, and is held by the annular ligament.
The ossicles are connected by two synovial joints, the incudomalleolar and the incudostapedial joint.

cumleler.yazi: A stiff chain can lead to a type As tympanogram, and a disrupted chain to a type Ad tympanogram.
cumleler.ses: A stiff chain can lead to a type A S tympanogram, and a disrupted chain to a type A D tympanogram.

sahneler.soru: Where does the stapes footplate sit?
sahneler.aciklama: The stapes footplate sits in the _fenestra vestibuli_ (oval window) and is held by the annular ligament.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: Which structure does the stapes footplate sit in?

cumleler: The correct answer is B, the oval window. The stapes footplate sits in the fenestra vestibuli and is held by the annular ligament.
